2026-07-31.headline: Note: 31 Jul figures are intraday prints. A data flag first, and this time it is a resolution rather than an exception: the extract's 29 Jul row, which never refreshed for yesterday's edition, has now been fully backfilled with true closes, and MOVE, VIX, SOFR and JGLA have all printed for 29 and 30 Jul. Both 29 and 30 Jul are therefore confirmed closes and every trigger test below runs off them. Score RISES to 26/30 — the US-inflation impulse fires 4→5 on two consecutive confirmed closes of 5Y5Y forward inflation above the 2.30% trigger (2.3302% on 29 Jul, 2.3303% on 30 Jul) — the first channel move in twelve sessions and the highest reading since 12 June. This is the upgrade the monitor flagged yesterday as the nearest available move, and it fired exactly as the discipline requires: an intraday break on 30 Jul, then confirmation, and only then the point. Five of six channels are now at or above 4 and four are maxed at 5. The second consequential line also went through. Stage-4 Threshold B — the 30Y above 5.20% with the 10Y above 4.65% — was satisfied on both legs on two consecutive confirmed closes (5.2007%/4.6773% on 29 Jul, 5.2135%/4.6733% on 30 Jul), the first time in the war. The 30Y close of 5.2135% is the highest in the series and 16.35 bp above the 13 May auction stop. Persistence is now the test, and the very first print after the trigger is a shade softer: this morning the 30Y eases to 5.1965%, 0.35 bp back beneath its leg, while the 10Y at 4.6531% stays 0.31 bp above. The tape this morning is a partial give-back of the post-FOMC repricing rather than a reversal of it. Yields are lower across the curve (2Y –1.1 bp, 10Y –2.0 bp, 30Y –1.7 bp), 5Y5Y slips 0.74 bp but holds 2.29 bp above its trigger for a third session, and crude gives back $0.92 to $85.96 with the active COA at $88.18. Two of yesterday's data gaps closed and both cut against the reassuring reading: MOVE resolved at 77.09 on the 30 Jul close, up 2.91 on the day and above the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade, so that downgrade is doubly dead; and Asia LNG backfilled to a rising ¥3,527, not a stale ¥3,418. The events kept deteriorating and still cannot register: CENTCOM ran a second consecutive night over Iran, describing a heavy wave against dozens of IRGC targets; an Iranian strike killed a worker in Kuwait, the first fatality on Kuwaiti soil; Jordan intercepted five more missiles; and Gharibabadi hardened again, from 'the strait will remain closed' to 'the strait will never return to its pre-war state.' Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 Jul, so none of it moves the number — the point that arrived today came from a US bond market repricing the Fed, not from Hormuz. That is the central fact of this edition and of the month now closing: July's damage was done to the long end. Sequencing 25 → 25 → 26.

Closed since 28 Feb; naval blockade plus escort operation unchanged. Traffic ticked up off the floor: Kpler counted 14 commodity vessels crossing in both directions on 29 Jul, up from single digits the previous week, and Windward logged 20 transits the same day (10 in / 10 out) of which four ran dark; the Gulf fleet is 812 vessels with 135 flagged high-risk. A SECOND NIGHT — CENTCOM heavy wave over Iran, 29–30 Jul

CENTCOM said it struck ‘dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities,’ framed as a response to Iran’s 28 Jul launches. A single retaliatory night has become a two-night sequence, which is the distinction between a cycle and a restarted campaign. Iranian state media reported a family of three killed by a strike on a home on Qeshm Island and further strikes on Ahvaz (Tier 3, casualty toll not independently verified). Cumulative US losses stand at 18 service members killed and more than 600 wounded.
CENTCOM 29 Jul / AP / Reuters / NYT / Al Jazeera / Middle East Eye / Press TV (Tier 3)
Iranian fire spreads — a first fatality in Kuwait

An Iranian strike hit a Chinese company’s building in northern Kuwait, killing one worker: the first death on Kuwaiti soil in the war. Jordan’s armed forces intercepted five more Iranian missiles with no casualties. The IRGC claimed an ‘Operation Nasr 2’ that destroyed drone hangars and a fuel depot at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait and three F-35s in Jordan; CENTCOM says all missiles were intercepted and the claims are uncorroborated (Tier 3).
Kuwait Defence Ministry via AP / Reuters / Arab News / Jordan (Petra) via AP / Press TV (Tier 3)
Mediation — Iran hardens again; Pakistan says talks continue

Gharibabadi moved from ‘the strait will remain closed’ to ‘the strait will never return to its pre-war state,’ demanding total control of the northern route and calling the southern Omani corridor illegal and unsafe. The IMO confirmed it is not party to the Iran–Oman talks and that any new routeing scheme needs formal member-state submission, so neither the Omani nor the Iranian plan currently has standing. Oman’s foreign minister convened Gulf counterparts on 29 Jul. The one positive thread: Pakistan’s foreign ministry said on 31 Jul that negotiations are ongoing and that it is working to return both sides to the June ‘Islamabad MoU.’ The IRGC said two tankers attempted the southern lane on 28 Jul, one caught fire and both turned back (Tier 3, no vessel names, unverified).
The National / Al Jazeera / Pakistan Today / Express Tribune / IMO / Press TV (Tier 3)
Energy infrastructure and the Red Sea

Aramco has told Reuters via Industrial Info that the 400k b/d Jizan complex stays offline until mid-August after a Houthi strike damaged its IGCC powerplant and tank farm. Satellite imagery reportedly shows burn scars across four of the six spheroids at Abqaiq; Aramco has not commented, and no throughput loss is verifiable. Saudi crude has been pushed off Bab al-Mandeb almost entirely since the 20 Jul Houthi embargo, with Suez-routed volume up 106% to 1.06 mb/d and voyage times going from ~24 to ~54 days. Bab al-Mandeb ran 21 commodity transits on 29 Jul, down from 38 the day before. Saudi Arabia launched a 14-nation Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance on 30 Jul — note its remit is the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb and Gulf of Aden, NOT Hormuz. Attribution for the 29 Jul Damietta drone strike on the Gaslog Salem and the US-owned Energos Winter is still unresolved; the Houthis denied it and unnamed Iranian sources told the NYT it was designed to show what deeper disruption would look like.

analysis.intro: The US economic shock rises to 26/30, its first move in twelve sessions and its highest reading since 12 June. The point did not come from Hormuz. It came from the US bond market, which spent the two sessions after the FOMC hold pricing a permanently higher inflation compensation into the long end, and it fired only once two confirmed closes were on the board. That sequencing matters: the monitor held this channel at 4 yesterday with the trigger 3.11 bp through on an intraday print, and took the point today when 29 and 30 Jul both closed above 2.30%. The same two closes satisfied Stage-4 Threshold B on both legs for the first time in the war. Meanwhile the geopolitical track got worse again — a second consecutive night of US strikes on Iran, a first fatality in Kuwait, five more missiles over Jordan, and Iran moving from 'the strait will remain closed' to 'the strait will never return to its pre-war state' — and none of it could move the number, because maritime and escalation have been maxed since 10 and 9 Jul. This morning's tape gives a little back: yields lower across the curve, crude down $0.92, the 30Y 0.35 bp under its Stage-4 leg. That is a partial retracement of a large repricing, not a reversal, and it is exactly the kind of print the persistence test exists to absorb.
analysis.bondYieldNote: 31 Jul yields are intraday. Both the 29 and 30 Jul rows are confirmed closes — yesterday's stale-row exception has resolved — and all trigger tests run off them. One channel moved: US inflation 4→5. Score 25→26.

bondYield.title: (i) US inflation impulse — UPGRADED 4→5. The trigger is confirmed.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed at 2.3302% on 29 Jul and 2.3303% on 30 Jul, two consecutive confirmed closes above the 2.30% upgrade line, with the 30 Jul close the highest reading in the series. That is the sustained break the trigger specifies, and it is the same standard that fired this channel 3→4 on 15 Jul on the second consecutive close above 2.20%. Yesterday the monitor held at 4 with the line 3.11 bp behind it on an intraday print and said one confirmed close would start the clock and a second would fire it; both arrived. This morning's 2.3229% is 2.29 bp above the trigger for a third session, so the upgrade is not resting on a single pair of closes. The corroboration is more mixed than it was: the 10Y breakeven has come back to 2.2566%, which is its 2.2569% pre-war anchor to three decimal places, after two sessions above. That divergence is itself informative — spot ten-year compensation is unchanged from before the war while the five-year forward five-year rate is 18.09 bp higher. The market is not pricing more inflation now; it is pricing a higher terminal inflation rate, which is precisely the kind of expectations damage a central bank cannot fix with a single hike. The mechanism remains the 29 Jul hold against three dissents for a tightening, from a Chair who has removed forward guidance and whose message is rhetorical rather than operational. Note also what did not do the work: June core PCE, released 30 Jul, was +0.1% m/m and +3.3% y/y, cooler than the 0.2% consensus on the month. Breakevens rose anyway. The downgrade (5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% anchor) is 18.09 bp away and not in play. At 5/5 this channel is now maxed and can only subtract from here.

bondYield.title: (ii) Treasury — held at 5; the downgrade now fails on both legs.
bondYield.text: The 30Y closed at 5.2135% on 30 Jul, the highest in the series, leaving 21.35 bp of cushion above the 5.00% downgrade leg; this morning's 5.1965% still leaves 19.65 bp. More important, the MOVE gap has closed and it closed the wrong way for the downgrade: 74.18 on the 29 Jul FOMC close, then 77.09 on 30 Jul, so rates vol is above the 75 leg, not below it. Yesterday the monitor recorded MOVE as unresolved rather than as reassurance and declined to claim it was 1.09 pts from release; that judgment holds up, though the intermediate detail is worth recording honestly — vol actually fell on decision day and only rose afterwards, so the inference that it 'has almost certainly risen' was right in net over two sessions but wrong about the FOMC session itself. The character of the move is unchanged and is the point: a bear steepener with breakevens up and the dollar down. Over July the 30Y is 26.2 bp higher, 2s10s is 12.9 bp steeper, and the dollar is 1.02 lower. This morning's small bull flattening — every tenor lower, the curve 1.0 bp flatter — is a month-end print, not a change of regime. September hike odds sit somewhere between 57% and 61% on the two independent CME FedWatch reads I can corroborate, up from 32–38% before the meeting; a 81% figure is circulating from a single non-financial outlet and is not used here.

bondYield.title: (iii) Oil — held at 2, and the striking thing is again how little crude is doing.
bondYield.text: The last confirmed close is $86.88 (30 Jul), $8.12 below the $95 upgrade trigger; this morning's $85.96 is $9.04 below it, a third consecutive lower print. Crude has now given back most of the strike-resumption bid even as the strikes ran a second night, Iran killed a worker in Kuwait and Tehran hardened its position on the strait to permanence. July was still a violent month for the barrel — +19.1% on the close basis, from $72.92 on 30 Jun to $86.88 — but the direction of travel in the last three sessions is down. The physical picture argues the other way: Jizan's 400k b/d refinery is out to mid-August, Abqaiq shows unexplained burn scars on four of six spheroids, Saudi crude has been forced off Bab al-Mandeb onto a 54-day Suez routing, and the IEA puts effective OPEC+ spare capacity at roughly 0.17 mb/d excluding shut-in Iranian and Russian barrels. Against that sit the offsets that have absorbed every escalation this month: OPEC+ is expected to approve a final +188k b/d for September at the 2 Aug meeting before pausing, and the IEA's members have released 290 mb since 11 March with over 1 bn bbl left. The US strategic cushion is the one that is visibly wearing out — the SPR fell another 3.7 mb to 307.7 mb in the week to 24 Jul, an eighteenth consecutive weekly draw and the lowest since 1983. The downgrade to 1 requires a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48; with Iran now saying the strait will never return to its pre-war state, the pause condition is remote and the downgrade is effectively unavailable even though the price leg is $13.48 away.

bondYield.title: (iv) Political — held at 4; the stall at the line is now four prints long.
bondYield.text: AUTMUSAG printed exactly $4.75 on 24, 27, 28 and 29 Jul and is blank for 30 and 31 Jul. The upgrade needs the series sustained ABOVE $4.75, and sitting on the line is not through it. The external cross-read continues to argue that the stall is real: AAA's separately published regular-grade national average was $4.098 on 30 Jul against $4.091 a week earlier, a gain of seven-tenths of a cent across a week in which crude traded from $82 to $88 and back. RBOB has come off its 23 Jul two-month high. The pass-through pipeline is still tight — crude stocks about 7% below the five-year average, gasoline stocks about 7% below, refinery utilisation last confirmed at 96.2% for the week to 17 Jul, the SPR at 307.7 mb — so a sustained crude leg higher would still reach the pump quickly. But it has not happened, and on the evidence the channel is more likely to be taken off its trigger by a sub-$4.75 backfill than through it. No federal intervention — SPR release, export limit, waiver or gouging action — is confirmable in the 29–31 Jul window.

analysis.stage4Note: Stage 4 is a credit/auction event. Threshold B, armed on an intraday print yesterday, is SATISFIED on confirmed closes today — the first time in the war. The persistence test now runs.

stage4.title: Threshold A · 13 May 30Y auction, cleared 5.050%.
stage4.text: Historical benchmark; the 9 Jul re-opening cleared 5.06% with a 0.3 bp stop-through. The 30 Jul close of 5.2135% is 16.35 bp above the May stop, the widest margin of the war. The supply test is now dated: Treasury publishes its quarterly marketable borrowing estimates on Monday 3 August and the refunding statement on Wednesday 5 August at 8:30am ET, with the 30Y refunding leg auctioning in the week of 10 August. The May refunding held sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn and guided to unchanged coupons 'for at least the next several quarters,' with dealers not expecting increases until early 2027. Any deviation from that guidance next week meets a long end that has just repriced 26 bp in a month.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — SATISFIED on two consecutive confirmed closes.
stage4.text: 29 Jul: 30Y 5.2007%, 10Y 4.6773%. 30 Jul: 30Y 5.2135%, 10Y 4.6733%. Both legs, both sessions. This is the first time in the war the threshold has been met on a close basis, and it is the single most consequential development in this edition after the score change itself. Two qualifications belong with it. First, the threshold is a warning that the long end is repricing in a way that historically precedes an auction or credit event; it is not itself a Stage-4 event, and Stage 4 requires the repricing to persist and then to show up in a failed or heavily tailed auction. Second, persistence is already being tested: this morning's 30Y at 5.1965% is 0.35 bp back beneath its leg, while the 10Y at 4.6531% holds 0.31 bp above. A close back under 5.20% tonight would leave B satisfied on two closes but not sustained — which is the same asymmetry the monitor applies to score channels, and the reason this is reported as a threshold met rather than a stage entered. The mechanism arming it is domestic monetary credibility, not a Hormuz headline.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130. Now evaluated, and far off.
stage4.text: The series resolved after two blank sessions: 74.18 on 29 Jul, 77.09 on 30 Jul. At 77.09 the index is 52.91 pts below the threshold and well under the 115.02 war high of 26 March. Recorded as far off — but note it is 3.71 above its pre-war level and above the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade, so the same number that makes C remote also makes that downgrade unavailable.

analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature is now unambiguous and it is domestic. Over the two sessions since the FOMC the long end repriced hard and the dollar fell: the 30Y closed at a series high 5.2135%, 2s10s steepened to +42.53 bp, 5Y5Y set a series high at 2.3303%, and DXY dropped 1.02 to 99.864 on 30 Jul, a much larger fall than yesterday's morning snapshot showed. Rates vol rose to 77.09 while equity vol collapsed to 17.09 as the S&P added 1.3% and the Nasdaq 2.3% — a split that says the stress is in duration, not in risk assets. This morning partially unwinds it: yields 1–2 bp lower across the curve, the dollar 0.30 higher, crude 0.92 lower, TTF 0.52 lower. The energy complex has been fading all week — Brent down three sessions running, TTF €5.85 off its war record, WTI back under $80 — while the rates complex did the damage. The one energy series still climbing is Asia LNG, which backfilled to ¥3,527 on 30 Jul, up ¥58 on the day and up ¥109 from the 28 Jul print that yesterday's edition had to leave hanging. Henry Hub at $2.758 remains 10.0% BELOW pre-war: the routing signature is intact and this is still not a global-energy shock. The month-end frame is the cleanest summary of July: Brent +19.1%, TTF +34.2%, the 30Y +26.2 bp, 2s10s +12.9 bp steeper, 5Y5Y +15.1 bp, and the dollar down 1.02. The war moved energy; the Fed moved the curve; and it is the curve that added the point today.

2026-07-31.scoreTotal: CRISIS band — UP one point, the first channel move in twelve sessions and the highest reading since 12 June. The point came from the US bond market, not from Hormuz: two confirmed closes of 5Y5Y above 2.30% took the US-inflation impulse to its maximum. Four of six channels are now at 5/5. With maritime, escalation, US-inflation and Treasury all maxed, only oil (2/5) and political (4/5) retain any upside — the scale now has just four points left in it.

methodology.scale: Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition is the payoff to that discipline rather than a cost of it. Yesterday 5Y5Y was 3.11 bp through its upgrade trigger on an intraday print and the channel held at 4; today two consecutive confirmed closes above 2.30% take it to 5 and the score to 26. 2026-08-03.headline: Note: 3 Aug figures are intraday prints; the last confirmed close is Friday 31 Jul. The integrity check clears — the 31 Jul row has refreshed properly and differs materially from the snapshot published for it, so it is a true close. Score HOLDS at 26/30 — all six channels unchanged (maritime 5, oil 2, US inflation 5, Treasury 5, political 4, escalation 5), but for the first time in the war the monitor carries a live downgrade candidate and a live upgrade candidate at the same time. Two things happened over the weekend and they point in opposite directions. First, and larger for markets: the US session on Friday, which the Singapore morning snapshot had missed, was a violent bear steepener. The 30Y closed at 5.2724%, the 10Y at 4.7347% and 5Y5Y forward inflation at 2.3597% — all three the highest readings of the war — and MOVE jumped 5.93 to 83.02, its highest since 19 May. Stage-4 Threshold B is now satisfied on a third consecutive confirmed close, and the 30Y sits 22.24 bp above the 13 May auction stop, the widest margin of the war, going into a refunding week. Second, and larger for the narrative: President Trump said on 2 Aug that he had cancelled a planned strike package he described as 'the biggest attack since World War II' and announced a new round of talks beginning Monday 3 Aug with Oman mediating. Iran immediately rejected the framing — Tehran denies asking for the pause, denies any Hormuz deal, calling the claim 'a new lie', and says what is actually near-final is a bilateral Iran–Oman negotiation on a NEW corridor, not a reopening of the old one. This is the first genuinely live downgrade candidate the escalation channel has had since it maxed on 9 July, and it is deliberately not taken today: the talks had not convened at the time of this snapshot, no principal has confirmed terms, an LNG carrier loaded with Qatari cargo was struck mid-transit on 31 Jul, UKMTO logged an explosion beside a tanker off Khasab on 2 Aug, and the hysteresis rule exists precisely to stop a channel moving on an announcement. Crude, characteristically, moved first and moved hard: Brent front-month prints $81.56 this morning, –$6.37 on the day and the largest single-session decline since 25 May, with OPEC+ having approved a final +188k b/d for September on 2 Aug. So the tape is now split cleanly in two. The energy complex is trading the diplomacy; the bond market is trading the Federal Reserve, and it set three war records on Friday doing it. Sequencing 25 → 26 → 26.

analysis.intro: The shock holds at 26/30 and the two halves of the tape have separated. On Friday, after the Singapore snapshot had closed, the US bond market set three war records in a single session: the 30Y at 5.2724%, the 10Y at 4.7347% and 5Y5Y forward inflation at 2.3597%, with MOVE up 5.93 to 83.02. Stage-4 Threshold B is satisfied on a third consecutive close and the 30Y is now 22.24 bp above the May auction stop with the quarterly refunding calendar landing this week. Over the weekend the geopolitical track went the other way: a planned US strike package was cancelled, talks were announced for today with Oman mediating, and no Tier 1 outlet reported a new strike on Iran in the window. Crude has taken that at face value — Brent front-month is $81.56 this morning, down $6.37 and the largest one-day fall since 25 May, helped by OPEC+ approving a final +188k b/d for September. The escalation channel is therefore, for the first time since 9 July, holding a live downgrade candidate rather than an unusable maximum. It is not taken this edition, for the same reason the US-inflation upgrade was not taken on 30 July: the evidence is one session old, the principals disagree about what was agreed, and the waterway was still being shot at while the announcement was made.

bondYield.title: (i) Treasury — held at 5, and Friday made the downgrade look further away, not closer.
bondYield.text: The 30Y closed at 5.2724% on 31 Jul, the highest of the war, 7.59 bp above my morning snapshot and 22.24 bp above the 13 May auction stop of 5.050%. The 10Y closed at 4.7347%, also a war record. Both downgrade legs now fail comprehensively: the 30Y is 27.24 bp above the 5.00% line on the close and 23.70 bp above it intraday, and MOVE at 83.02 is 8.02 pts above the 75 leg after rising 5.93 in a session. This morning gives back a few basis points across the curve — 2Y –4.6 bp, 5Y –4.6 bp, 10Y –4.1 bp, 30Y –3.5 bp — but that is a partial retracement of a 10 bp weekly move in the long end, and the curve continued to steepen through it: 2s10s at +44.6 bp is the steepest since 26 May. The character has not changed since the FOMC: a bear steepener with breakevens up and the dollar down to its lowest since 16 June. What makes this edition different from the last is the calendar. Treasury publishes its quarterly marketable borrowing estimates today and the refunding statement on Wednesday 5 August, with the 30Y refunding leg auctioning in the week of 10 August, into a long end that has just set a war high.

bondYield.title: (ii) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and confirmed rather than faded.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed at 2.3597% on 31 Jul, the highest reading of the war and a fourth consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger that fired this channel 4→5 on Friday. The upgrade taken last edition is not resting on a marginal pair of closes: the series has now printed 2.3302%, 2.3303%, 2.3597% and 2.3367% across four sessions, the last of them intraday. The 10Y breakeven has moved with it, closing at 2.2846% on 31 Jul, its highest since 3 July, and printing 2.2787% this morning — back above the 2.2569% pre-war anchor after touching it exactly a session earlier. That is a meaningful change from Friday’s reading, when spot compensation sat on its anchor while only the forward was elevated: now both are above pre-war, which narrows the case that this is purely a terminal-rate story and widens the case that near-term inflation compensation is rebuilding too. Note what is NOT doing the work. June core PCE, released 30 July, was +0.1% m/m against a +0.2% consensus. OPEC+ has just added barrels. Crude is $13.44 below the $95 trigger. Breakevens rose anyway, through a cool core print and a falling oil price, which is close to a controlled experiment in what markets think the Fed will tolerate. The downgrade — 5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% anchor — is 21.8 bp away on the last close and is not in play. At 5/5 the channel can only subtract.

bondYield.title: (iii) Oil — held at 2, and this is the channel the weekend actually moved.
bondYield.text: The last confirmed close is $87.93 (31 Jul), $7.07 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $1.05 above the Thursday close — Friday’s US session bought crude back, $1.97 above my morning print. Then the weekend happened. Brent front-month opens the week at $81.56, down $6.37, the largest single-session decline since 25 May and the lowest level since 10 July; WTI is $78.42, back under $80; the Brent–WTI spread has collapsed from $6.44 on Friday’s close to $3.14, which says the market is unwinding a Hormuz-specific premium rather than repricing global demand. Two causes, both dated 2 August: the cancelled strike package with talks announced for today, and OPEC+ approving a final +188k b/d for September that completes the unwind of the 1.65 mb/d voluntary tranche. The counter-argument is that neither cause changes a barrel of physical supply. Effective OPEC+ spare capacity was roughly 0.17 mb/d on the IEA’s July estimate, so September’s increment is a quota, not a cargo. Jizan’s 400k b/d is still out to mid-August. Abqaiq still shows unexplained burn scars. The strait is still closed on day ~157, still running at roughly a tenth of normal traffic, and an LNG carrier was still hit in it on 31 July. The channel stays at 2 because $87.93 is not $95; but the risk to that score is now genuinely two-sided for the first time since early July, and the downgrade leg — a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48 — has acquired a live first condition even though the price leg is $9.08 away.

bondYield.title: (iv) Political — held at 4, and it is now one print from firing.
bondYield.text: AUTMUSAG backfilled 30 July at $4.76 — the first print ABOVE the $4.75 trigger and the highest since 10 June — after four consecutive sessions exactly on the line. Then the series went dark for 31 July and 3 August. The upgrade rule requires a sustained break, which this monitor has consistently read as two consecutive confirmed closes; there is one. The channel therefore holds at 4 with the upgrade armed rather than fired, which is exactly the position the US-inflation channel occupied on 30 July before it fired the next day. The corroborating evidence is genuinely mixed. AAA’s separately published regular-grade national average was $4.098 on 30 July against $4.091 a week earlier, seven-tenths of a cent, which reads as a stall. But on-highway diesel rose 17.9 cents in the week to 27 July against gasoline’s 9.5 cents, and on 1 August both Exxon and Chevron told the market that refining, not crude, is the binding constraint — roughly a tenth of global refining capacity is offline, Chevron’s chief executive called middle distillates ‘the real pain point’ and expects upward pressure on product prices into the third quarter. That is a mechanism by which the pump can keep rising even as Brent falls $6, and it is why a $6 fall in crude this morning should not be read as taking the political channel off its trigger. No federal intervention — SPR release, export limit, waiver or gouging action — is confirmable in the window.

stage4.title: Threshold A · 13 May 30Y auction, cleared 5.050%.
stage4.text: Historical benchmark; the 9 July re-opening cleared 5.06% with a 0.3 bp stop-through. The 31 July close of 5.2724% is 22.24 bp above the May stop, the widest margin of the war, up from 16.35 bp a session earlier. stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — SATISFIED on three consecutive confirmed closes.
stage4.text: 29 July: 5.2007% / 4.6773%. 30 July: 5.2135% / 4.6733%. 31 July: 5.2724% / 4.7347%, both war records. The persistence question raised last edition has been answered in the affirmative, and answered by the widest margin yet: Friday’s 30Y was 7.24 bp through its leg and the 10Y 8.47 bp through its own, against 1.35 bp and 0.33 bp on Thursday. This morning’s intraday prints of 5.2370% and 4.6939% keep both legs satisfied on a fourth session. The qualification that belongs with it is unchanged: the threshold is a warning that the long end is repricing in a way that historically precedes an auction or credit event, not a Stage-4 event in itself. Stage 4 requires this to show up in a failed or heavily tailed auction, and the calendar now supplies the test within nine days. The mechanism arming it remains domestic monetary credibility, not a Hormuz headline — which is why the weekend’s de-escalation moved crude $6 and did not move the long end at all.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130. Far off, but moving the wrong way.
stage4.text: The index closed at 83.02 on 31 July, up 5.93 on the session and the highest since 19 May. That leaves 46.98 pts to the threshold and it remains well under the 115.02 war high of 26 March, so C is not close. Two things are worth recording anyway: rates volatility has now risen in three of the last four sessions and is 9.64 pts above its pre-war level, and at 83.02 it is 8.02 pts above the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade, so the same reading that keeps C remote keeps that downgrade unavailable. There is no 3 August print; the number is flagged and not carried as fresh.

analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature has split in two, and the split is the story of this edition. The bond market spent Friday doing damage: the 30Y closed at a war-record 5.2724%, the 10Y at a war-record 4.7347%, 5Y5Y at a war-record 2.3597%, the 10Y breakeven at its highest since 3 July, MOVE up 5.93 to 83.02 and 2s10s steepening to +43.94 bp. The energy complex spent the weekend doing the opposite: Brent front-month down $6.37 to $81.56, WTI back under $80, TTF at €56.30 and its lowest since 16 July, Asia LNG turning lower to ¥3,440 on Friday. Two markets, two views: equities and crude are pricing a war that ends at a negotiating table in Oman, while the long end is pricing a central bank that has lost the inflation argument and a Treasury that has to fund itself on Wednesday. Henry Hub at $2.766 remains 9.7% BELOW pre-war, so the routing signature is intact and this is still not a global-energy shock. If the talks that opened today hold, the oil channel and the escalation channel can both fall. Nothing in Oman fixes the 30-year.

methodology.scale: Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger; escalation-risk and maritime denial are event-based. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition applies that rule twice and in both directions, which is unusual. Political stress printed $4.76 on 30 July, its first reading above the $4.75 trigger, and holds at 4 because one close is not a sustained break — the identical position the US-inflation channel occupied on 30 July before firing on 31 July. Escalation risk holds at 5 despite a cancelled US strike package and an announced negotiation, because an announcement is not a stand-down, the principals publicly disagree about what was agreed, and an LNG carrier was struck in the strait on 31 July. The precedent that governs is 25–26 June, when an oil downgrade was taken on one session’s evidence and had to be reversed the next day.
methodology.scaleCap: Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 July, and US inflation and Treasury joined them at the ceiling on 31 July and 14 July. Four of six channels are maxed, so only oil (2/5) and political stress (4/5) can raise the number — four points of range in a 30-point scale. The novelty this edition is that the cap now also hides improvement: a genuine de-escalation began over the weekend and the score could not fall either, because the escalation channel needs a sustained stand-down before it can move off its maximum. Readers should treat a flat number from here as evidence that the scale is saturated in both directions, not as evidence that nothing changed.
